\section{Ising model \sphinxhyphen{} Notes}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:ising-model-notes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:statistical-mechanics-ising-notes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes::doc}}

\subsection{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:introduction}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:statistical-mechanics-ising-introduction}}

\subsection{Time evolution}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:time-evolution}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:statistical-mechanics-ising-time-evolution}}

\subsubsection{Metropolis\sphinxhyphen{}Hastings}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:metropolis-hastings}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Metropolis\sphinxhyphen{}Hastings algorithm is designed to generate a collection of states according to a desired distribution \(p(s)\), using a \sphinxstylestrong{Markov process} with a unique \sphinxstylestrong{stationary distribution} \(\pi(s) = p(s)\).
\subsubsection*{Algorithm}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initialize state \(s_0\) with energy \(E_0\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
while \sphinxstylestrong{not} terminal condition:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flip the spin of a randomly chosen site, to get the possible state \(s_\widetilde{n}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
calculate the change in energy of the state \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n := \widetilde{E}_n - E_{n-1}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
update state:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n < 0\) accept the change, \(s_n = s_{\widetilde{n}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\Delta \widetilde{E}_n > 0\) accept the change with probability \(\exp\left( - \frac{\Delta \widetilde{E}_n}{T} \right)\)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting from the \sphinxstylestrong{detailed balance} (sufficient but not necessary condition for the existence of a (unique?) stationary state), \(P(s'|s) p(s) = P(s|s') p(s')\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{P(s'|s)}{P(s|s')} = \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
each transition is splitted in \sphinxstylestrong{two sub\sphinxhyphen{}steps}: proposal and acceptance\sphinxhyphen{}rejection steps. Transition is written as \(P(s'|s) = g(s'|s) A(s',s)\) being \(g(s'|s)\) the proposal conditional probability, and \(A(s',s)\) the acceptance probability. Acceptance probability is choosen in a way to satisfy the conditions of time\sphinxhyphen{}reversal and ergodicity. Metropolis choice reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A(s', s) = \min \left( 1, \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \frac{g(s|s')}{g(s'|s)} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{check if Metropolis choice fulfills the necessary conditions.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example: Boltmann distribution with uniform proposal.} Let a system have Boltzmann stationary distribution, \(p(s) \propto \exp\left( - \beta E(s) \right)\), and uniform proposal conditional probability \(g(s'|s) = \frac{1}{N}\), with \(N\) the number of accessible states from the state \(s\).
\label{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 11.1.1 (Ising model on a 2D lattice with 1 flip per update)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, for an Ising model on a 2D lattice with dimension \(m \times n\) with proposal update with \(1\) flip \(N = mn\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/statistical-mechanics/ising-notes:example-1}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 11.1.2 (Ising model on a 2D lattice with \protect\(k\protect\) flips per update)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Is a probability built with independent successive flips ok? Target states at each flip have the same probability, s.t. the probability of reaching steps \(s_k\) after \(k\) flips starting from \(s_0\) is not uniform.}


\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(g(s|s') = g(s'|s)\). The acceptance probability of the transition between different states \(s' \ne s\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A(s',s) = \min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the corresponding element of transition matrix is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(s'|s) = \frac{1}{N} \min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{diagonal elements} of the probability transition matrix \sphinxhyphen{} representing no state transition \sphinxhyphen{} are evaluated as the probability that makes \(\sum_{s'} P(s'|s) = P(s|s) + \sum_{s' \in T(s)} P(s'|s) = 1\), i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(s|s) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\begin{aligned} s' & \in T(s) \\ E(s') & > E(s) \end{aligned}} \left( 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right)  \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(P(s|s)\protect\)}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  P(s|s) 
  & = 1 - \sum_{s' \in T(s)} P(s'|s) = \\
  & = 1 - \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \frac{1}{N} \min \left( 1, e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \left[ 1 - \min \left( 1, e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) \right] = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{s' \in T(s)} \max \left( 0, 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\begin{aligned} s' & \in T(s) \\ E(s') & > E(s) \end{aligned}} \left( 1 - e^{-\beta (E(s') - E(s))} \right)  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It’s easy to prove that this probability functions are related by the detailed balance equations,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{P(s'|s)}{P(s|s')} = \frac{\min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } \right) }{\min \left( 1, e^{ -\beta ( E(s) - E(s') )  } \right) } = e^{ -\beta ( E(s') - E(s) )  } = \frac{e^{-\beta E(s')}}{e^{-\beta E(s)}} = \frac{p(s')}{p(s)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Markov processes}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:markov-processes}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/rl/mdp.html}{\sphinxstylestrong{Markov Process.}} Let \(S\) a finite set of state \(s\) that can be indexed with integer indices \(i\), \(P\) the transition probability between two states at consecutive time\sphinxhyphen{}steps, \(P_{ss'} = P(s'|s)\), and \(p_0\) the initial probability. A Markox process is uniquely defined by the triple
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\langle S, P, p_0 \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the Markov process is \sphinxstylestrong{time\sphinxhyphen{}homogeneous}, state transition matrix \(P\) is independent from the time\sphinxhyphen{}step.


\subsection{State transition matrix}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:state-transition-matrix}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-transition-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the finite set of states with integer indices, their probabilities at time \(n\) can be collected in the \(|S|\)\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional vector \(\mathbf{p}_n\). Transition from time \(n-1\) to \(n\) can be represented as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n(s') = \sum_s P (s'|s) p_{n-1}(s) = \sum_s P_{ss'} p_{n-1}(s)  \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or using matrix formalism
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}^T_{n} = \mathbf{p}^T_{n-1} \mathbf{P} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(\mathbf{p}_n\) and \(\mathbf{P}\) represents probability, their elements are non\sphinxhyphen{}negative. As the \(i^{th}\) element of \(\mathbf{p}_n\) represents the probability of the system of being in state \(i\) at time \(n\), it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_i \left\{ \mathbf{p}_n \right\}_i = \sum_i p_n(i) = 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the element \(P_{ij} = P(i|j)\) represents the conditional probability of reaching \(j\) from state \(i\) in one step, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_{j} \left\{ \mathbf{P} \right\}_{ij} = \sum_j P(j|i) = 1 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Properties}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:properties}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-properties}}

\subsubsection{Eigenvalue \protect\(s = 1\protect\), and stationary state \protect\(\ \boldsymbol\pi\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:eigenvalue-s-1-and-stationary-state-boldsymbol-pi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum of the elements of each row of \(\mathbf{P}\) is equal to \(1\), as \(\sum_{s'} P_{ss'} = \sum_{s'} P(s' | s) = 1\). Equivalently, state transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\), with the uniform right eigenvector \(\mathbf{1}\), i.e. \(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The corresponding left eigenvector is a stationary state \(\boldsymbol\pi\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boldsymbol\pi^T \mathbf{P} = \boldsymbol\pi^T \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Spectrum of the transition matrix and asymptotic behavior of the system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:spectrum-of-the-transition-matrix-and-asymptotic-behavior-of-the-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Are all the transition matrices diagonalizable?}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming the transition matrix can be diagonalized, the evolution of the system from the initial probability \(\mathbf{p}_0\) can be easily represented. The initial probabbility is written as \(\mathbf{p}_0 = c_k \mathbf{w}_k\), being \(\mathbf{w}_k\) the left eigenvectors of the transition matrix, and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{p}^T_n
  =\mathbf{p}^T_{n-1} \mathbf{P}
  =\mathbf{p}^T_{0} \underbrace{\mathbf{P} \dots \mathbf{P}}_{ n \text{ times} }
  =a_k \underbrace{\mathbf{w}^T_k \mathbf{P}}_{= \lambda_k \mathbf{w}_k^T} \dots \mathbf{P}
  =a_k \lambda_k^n \mathbf{w}_k^T \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As \(n \rightarrow +\infty\) only the contributions of the eigenvectors with \(|\lambda_k| = 1\) survive. If there’s only one of these eigenvalues, \(\lambda_1 = 1\), the system converges to \(\mathbf{1}\). If there are many eigenvalues with \(\lambda_i = 1\), there system converges with probability \(a_i\) to those stationary states, being \(a_i\) the component of the initial state of the system along the \(i^{th}\) eigenvector,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}_n \sim a_k \mathbf{w}_k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Detailed balance}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:detailed-balance}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/markov-process-notes:statistical-mechanics-markov-process-properties-detailed-balance}}

By definition, a \sphinxstylestrong{reversible Markov chain} has a positive stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi\) that satisfies the detailed balance equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the flow between each pair of states \(i\), \(j\) is individaully balanced. Reversibility is a sufficient \sphinxhyphen{} even not necessary \sphinxhyphen{} condition for the existence of a stationary state.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\pi_i \ne 0\) for \(\forall i\), it’s possible to define a symmetric matrix via a similarity transformation, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \sqrt{\pi_i}\sqrt{\pi_i} P_{ij} & = \sqrt{\pi_j}\sqrt{\pi_j} P_{ji} \\
  \sqrt{\pi_i} P_{ij} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi_j}} & = \sqrt{\pi_j} P_{ji} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi_i}} \\
  S_{ij} & = S_{ji} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{D} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{D}^{-1}\), with \(\mathbf{D} = \text{diag}\{ \sqrt{\pi_i} \}\). As the matrices \(\mathbf{P}\) and \(\mathbf{S}\) are related via a similarity transformation, they have the same eigenvalues

The relation between state probability \(P(E)\) \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. probability of getting a microstate with energy \(E\) \sphinxhyphen{}, degeneracy number \(g(E)\) \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the number of microstates with energy \(E\) \sphinxhyphen{} and the Boltzmann distribution \(\propto e^{-\beta E}\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P(E) = \frac{g(E) e^{-\beta E}}{Z} = \frac{g(E) e^{-\beta E}}{\sum_{E'} g(E') e^{-\beta E'}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the value \(E\) of energy levels is known, the exponential is known. Probability \(P(E)\) is sampled from experiments. Thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{g(E)}{Z} = P(E) e^{\beta E} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the total number of microstate is not known, \(g(E)\) can be evaluated up to a multiplicative constant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the total number of microstates is known, \(\sum_E g(E) = N\), it’s possible to compute all the values of \(g(E)\) and \(Z\). In this case, a linear system reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases} 
  g(E) = Z P(E) e^{\beta E} \\ \\
  \displaystyle\sum_{E'} g(E') = N \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  Z = \frac{N}{\sum_{E'} P(E') e^{\beta E'}} \quad , \quad
  g(E) = \frac{N P(E) e^{\beta E}}{\sum_{E'} P(E') e^{\beta E'}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Log to avoid numerical exceptions.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ln g(E) = \ln Z + \ln P(E) + \beta E\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to evaluate \(Z\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_{E} g(E) e^{-\beta E} = \sum_{E} e^{\ln g(E) - \beta E} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and avoid overflow, the largest contribution is factored using the relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ln \sum_i e^{x_i} = \ln \left( e^{x_{max}} \sum_i  e^{-(x_{max}-x_i)} \right) = \ln e^{x_{max}} + \ln \sum_i e^{-(x_{max} - x_i )} = x_{max} +  \ln \sum_i e^{-(x_{max} - x_i )} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The largest exponential corresponds to energy value \(E_0\) at the maximum of \(P(E)\) as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E_0
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \left( \ln g(E) - \beta E \right) =  \\
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \left( \ln Z + \ln P(E) \right) =  \\
  & = \text{argmax}_{E} \ln P(E) = \\
  & = \text{argmax}_E P(E) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Then the value of the partition function becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Z = \sum_E e^{\ln g(E) - \beta E} = \ln g(E_0) - \beta E_0 + \sum_E e^{- \Delta \left( \ln g(E) - \beta E \right)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
begin \(\Delta f = f(E) - f(E_0)\), and \(E_0\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(N\) is known, \(N = \sum_E g(E)\)

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Entropy and arrow of time}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:entropy-and-arrow-of-time}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:statistical-mechanics-entropy}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Microscopic view vs. macroscopic view.} Usually we don’t know it accurately/we don’t care to know it, and summarize it with a macroscopic view: in this description some information is lost

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Microscopic symmetry, with uniform transition matrix

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many microstates correspond to the same macrostate

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the system evolves, its macrostate may evolve towards a stationary state, corrsponding with the macrostate with the most microstates. This evolution has a preferred direction \sphinxhyphen{} defining an \sphinxstylestrong{arrow of time} \sphinxhyphen{}, the one with \sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}decreasing} expected \sphinxstylestrong{entropy}. This evolution can also be described in terms of \sphinxstylestrong{increasing ignorance}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A macroscopic equilibrium corresponds to a stationary distribution of the macrostates with quite sharp maximum. While the macroscopic view looks stationary, the system is still evolving at the microscopic level. The amplitude of oscillations around an equilibrium decreases as \(\sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\)

\end{itemize}


\section{Box occupation example}
\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:box-occupation-example}}\label{\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:statistical-mechanics-entropy-box-occupation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} In this example, the microscopic dynamics of the system is not deterministic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A box with two rooms contains \(N\) chambers. This balls are numbered so that they are distingushable if you can see their labels.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Macrostate definition.} A macrostate of the system is defined here by the number of balls in each room, \((N_L, N_R)\). As the total number of balls is given and constant, the number of balls in one chamber, e.g. \(N_L\) in the left chamber, is enough to determine the macrostate being \(N_R = N - N_L\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Microstate counting.} The number of microstates producing the macrostate \(N_L\) is the number of combinations, \(C_{N, N_L}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Omega(N_L) = C_{N, N_L} = \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ N_L \end{matrix} \right) = \frac{N!}{(N-N_L)! N_L!} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy of a macrostate.} …
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S(n) = \ln \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Probability transition between macrostates.} Being the probability uniform for any transition of microstates, the probability of transition between macrostates reads
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:eq:entropy:box:trans-prob}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  P_{-}(n) := P(n \rightarrow n-1) & = \frac{n}{N} \\
  P_{+}(n) := P(n \rightarrow n+1) & = \frac{N-n}{N} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Expected change of entropy.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] 
  & = \sum_{i} P_i(n) \Delta S_i(n) = \\
  & = P_{-}(n) \left( S(n-1) - S(n) \right) + P_{+}(n) \left( S(n+1) - S(n) \right) = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n-1 \end{matrix} \right) }{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) } + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n+1 \end{matrix} \right) }{\left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) } = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} \frac{(N-n)!n!}{N!} + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} \frac{(N-n)!n!}{N!} = \\
  & = \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n)!n!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} + \frac{N-n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n)! n!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} = \\
  & = \ln \frac{(N-n)! n!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} = \\
  & = \ln \frac{(N-n)}{n+1} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{n (n+1)}{(N-n)(N-n+1)} = \\
  & = \dots
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{keep going with the algebra without the limit of large number of particles…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{In the limit} \(N \gg 1\), \(n \gg 1\), \(N-n \gg 1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] 
  & \simeq \ln \frac{N-n}{n} + \frac{n}{N} \ln \frac{n^2}{(N-n)^2} = \\
  & =      \ln \frac{N-n}{n} - \frac{2n}{N} \ln \frac{N-n}{n} = \\
  & =      \left( 1 - 2 \frac{n}{N} \right) \ln \frac{1 - \frac{n}{N}}{\frac{n}{N}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both factors change sign when \(\frac{n}{N} = \frac{1}{2}\). For \(\frac{n}{N} < \frac{1}{2}\) both factors are positive, for \(\frac{n}{N} > \frac{1}{2}\) both factors are negative. Thus, the expected variation of entropy of this process is non\sphinxhyphen{}negative for every value of \(n \in [0,N]\) and thus for every transition,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta S(n) \right] \ge 0 \ , \quad \forall n \in [0,N] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Markov process of macrostates.} The macrostates and the transition between them can be model as a stationary \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/rl/mdp.html}{Markov process}. The probability of the system of being in (macro)state \(n\) at time \(t\) is \(p_n(t)\), and using the transition probability \(P(n|m)\) from state \(m\) at \(t-1\) to state \(n\) at \(t\), the following holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n(t) = \sum_{m} P(n|m) p_m(t-1) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or using matrix formalism, introducing transition probability matrix \(\left\{\mathbf{P}\right\}_{mn} := P(n|m)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{p}(t-1) \mathbf{P} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The transition probabilities \eqref{equation:ch/statistical-mechanics/entropy:eq:entropy:box:trans-prob} define the elements of the transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{P} = \begin{bmatrix}
\cdot       & 1           &               &               &               &             &             \\ 
\frac{1}{N} & \cdot       & 1-\frac{1}{N} &               &               &             &             \\ 
            & \frac{2}{N} & \cdot         & 1-\frac{2}{N} &               &             &             \\ 
            &             & \dots         & \cdot         &         \dots &             &             \\ 
            &             &               & 1-\frac{2}{N} &         \cdot & \frac{2}{N} &             \\ 
            &             &               &               & 1-\frac{1}{N} & \cdot       & \frac{1}{N} \\ 
            &             &               &               &               & 1           & \cdot       \\ 
\end{bmatrix} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Stationary distribution.} The stationary distribution \(\mathbf{p}^*\) is invariant under a transition, i.e. it satisfies \(\mathbf{p}^* = \mathbf{p}^* \mathbf{P}\). The stationary distribution of the process is the Binomial distribution
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p^*_n = \frac{1}{2^N} \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be proved by direct computation. The first element reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_0^* = \frac{1}{N} p_1^* \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{2^N} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{N} \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{1}{N} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(n^{th}\) element (\(n \in (1,N-1)\)) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p_n^* = \left( 1-\frac{n-1}{N} \right) p_{n-1}^* + \frac{n+1}{N} p_{n+1}^* \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!}
 & = \left( 1 - \frac{n-1}{N} \right) \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)! (n-1)!} + \frac{n+1}{N} \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)! (n+1)!} = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \left[ \frac{N-n+1}{N} \frac{N!}{(N-n+1)!(n-1)!} + \frac{n+1}{N} \frac{N!}{(N-n-1)!(n+1)!} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!} \left[ \frac{n}{N} + \frac{N-n}{N} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2^N} \frac{N!}{(N-n)!n!} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Statistics of the stochastic process.} …

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Statistics of the stationary distribution.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average \(\mu = \frac{N}{2}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Variance \(\sigma^2 = \frac{N}{4}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Standard deviation  \(\sigma = \frac{\sqrt{N}}{2}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the relative fluctuation around the average can be estimated with the ratio of the standard deviation and the average value,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\sigma}{\mu} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so, the relative fluctuation decreases as \(N\) increases.

\subsubsection*{Average of a binomial distribution}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[n]
  & = \sum_{n=0}^{N} n \, p_n^* = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} \sum_{n=0}^{N} n \left( \begin{matrix} N \\ n \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} N \left( \begin{matrix} N-1 \\ n-1 \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \left( \begin{matrix} N-1 \\ n \end{matrix} \right) = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2^N} N 2^{N-1} = \frac{N}{2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Variance of a binomial distribution}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma^2_n = \mathbb{E}[n^2] - \left( \mathbb{E}[n] \right)^2 \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}[n^2] = \mathbb{E}[n(n-1)] + \mathbb{E}[n] \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the first term follows from a similar procedure as the one used for the average, using the identity \(n(n-1)\left(\begin{matrix} N \\n \end{matrix}\right) = N(N-1) \left( \begin{matrix} N-2 \\ n-2 \end{matrix} \right)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{E}[n(n-1)] = \frac{N(N-1)}{4} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the variance reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma^2_n = \frac{N(N-1)}{4} + \frac{N}{2} - \frac{N^2}{4} = \frac{N}{4} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Markov process of microstates.} A microstate is defined by the id of the box of each of the \(N\) balls. One\sphinxhyphen{}step transition switch the index of one ball. If the transition probability between these microstates is uniform it has probability \(\frac{1}{N}\). Not, let’s consider two states \(i\), \(j\). If these states are adjacent, the probabilities \(P^{micro}(i \rightarrow j) = P^{micro}(j \rightarrow i) = \frac{1}{N}\), and zero otherwise. Thus, the transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}^{micro}\) between microstates is symmetric. Since the \sphinxstylestrong{transition matrix is symmetric}, the \sphinxstylestrong{stationary distribution is uniform}. This is immediately proved using the normalization condition \(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\), and the definition of a stationary distribution, \(\mathbf{p}^{* T} = \mathbf{p}^{* T} \mathbf{P}\), and the definition of symmetric transition matrix \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}^T\). The transpose of the definition of the stationary distribution, \(\mathbf{p}^* = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{p}^*\), compared with the normalization condition, provides the relation \(\mathbf{p}^* = \alpha \mathbf{1}\), and normalization condition \(1 = |\mathbf{p}^*|_1 = \alpha N\), and \(\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\). The stationary distribution for the symmetric Markov process is \(\mathbf{p}^* = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{1}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea-hs/ch/statistics/combinatorics.html}{Combinatorics} naturally links the distribution of microstates and the distribution of the macrostates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{H\sphinxhyphen{}Theorem for symmetric Markov chains.} A discrete version of the Boltzmann’s H\sphinxhyphen{}Theorem exists for symmetric Markov process, assessing that the entropy \(H(\mathbf{p}(t)) := - \sum_k p_k(t) \ln p_k(t)\) is non\sphinxhyphen{}decreasing, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(\mathbf{p}(t+1)) \ge H(\mathbf{p}(t)) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} A generic transition probability matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) satisfies the normalization condition \(\sum_j P_{ij} = 1\), for every \(i\) (row sum). For a symmetric probability matrix \(\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}^T\), also the column sum holds \(\sum_i P_{ij} = 1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The function \(f(x) = x \ln x\) is convex, i.e. \(f''(x) > 0\), for \(x > 0\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  f' (x) & = \ln x + 1 \\
  f''(x) & = \frac{1}{x} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  H(t+1) 
  & = - \sum_k p_k(t+1) \ln p_k(t+1) = \\
  & = - \sum_k f( p_k(t+1) ) = \\
  & = - \sum_k f \left( \sum_i p_i(t) P_{ik} \right) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jensen’s Inequality.} As \(f\) is convex, and \(\sum_{i} P_{ik} = 1\), with \(P_{ik} \in (0,1)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f \left( \sum_i p_i P_{ik}  \right) \le \sum_i P_{ik} f( p_i ) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Jensen’s inequality in the expression of \(H(t+1)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
H(t+1)
 & \ge - \sum_k \sum_i P_{ik} f(p_i) = \\
 & = - \sum_i f(p_i) \underbrace{\sum_k P_{ik}}_{=1} 
   = H(t) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. \(H(t+1) \ge H(t)\).

\section{Mathematical tools for quantum mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:mathematical-tools-for-quantum-mechanics}}\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.1 (Operator)}


\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Adjoint Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.2 (Adjoint operator)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Given an operator \(\hat{A}: U \rightarrow V\), its adjoint operator \(\hat{A}^*: V \rightarrow U\) is the operator s.t.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(\mathbf{v}, \ \hat{A} \mathbf{u})_{V} = (\mathbf{u}, \hat{A}^* \mathbf{v} )_{U}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
holds for \(\forall \mathbf{u} \in U, \ \mathbf{v} \in V\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:Self-Adjoint Operator}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Definition 13.1.3 (Hermitian (self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint) operator)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
The operator \(\hat{A}: U \rightarrow U\) is a self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint operator if
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{A}^* = \hat{A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Self\sphinxhyphen{}adjoint operators have real eigenvalues, and orthogonal eigenvectors (at least those associated to different eigenvalues; those associated with the same eigenvalues can be used to build an orthogonal set of vectors with orthogonalization process).

\item {}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(|\Psi_i^A|^2\) that can be interpreted as the probability of finding the system in state \(|\Psi_i^a\rangle\)

\sphinxAtStartPar

            & = \langle \Psi | \left( \sum_i a_i | A_i \rangle \langle A_i | \right) | \Psi \rangle = \\

\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
since an operator \(\hat{A}\) can be written as a function of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors

\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

\end{equation*}

being \(\hat{H}\) the Hamiltonian operator and \(|\Psi\rangle\) the wave function, as a function of time \(t\) as an independent variable.


\subsubsection{Stationary States}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:stationary-states}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Eigenspace of the Hamiltonian operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} |\Psi_k \rangle = E_k |\Psi_k \rangle \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(E_k\) possible values of energy measurements. \sphinxstyleemphasis{If no eigenstates with the same eigenvalue exists, then…otherwise…}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Without external influence} \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{be more detailed!}, energy values and eigenstates of the systems are constant in time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, exapnding the state of the system \(|\Psi\rangle\) over the stationary states gives \(|\Psi_k\rangle\), \(|\Psi\rangle = |\Psi_k\rangle c_k(t)\), and inserting in Schrodinger equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{c}_k |\Psi_k\rangle = c_k  E_k |\Psi_k\rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and exploiting orthogonality of eigenstates, a diagonal system for the amplitudes of stationary states ariese,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i \hbar \dot{c}_k = c_k E_k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
whose solution reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_k(t) = c_{k,0} \exp \left[- i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the state of the system evolves like a superposition of monochromatic waves with frequencies \(\omega_k = \frac{E_k}{\hbar}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle = | \Psi_k \rangle c_k(t) = | \Psi_k \rangle c_{k,0}\exp\left[-i \frac{E_k}{\hbar} t \right] \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{d}{dt} \bar{A}
 & = \dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle \right) = \\
 & = \dfrac{d}{dt} \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle + \langle \Psi | \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} | \Psi \rangle + \langle \Psi | \hat{A} \frac{d}{dt} | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \langle \Psi | \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} | \Psi \rangle + \frac{i}{\hbar} \langle \Psi | \hat{H} \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle - \frac{i}{\hbar} \langle \Psi | \hat{A} \hat{H} | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \langle \Psi | \left( \frac{i}{\hbar} [ \hat{H}, \hat{A} ] + \frac{d \hat{A}}{dt} \right) | \Psi \rangle \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Schrodinger}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:schrodinger}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\hat{H}\) not function of time
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle (t) = \exp\left[ - i \frac{\hat{H}}{\hbar} (t-t_0) \right] | \Psi \rangle(t_0) = \hat{U}(t,t_0) | \Psi \rangle(t_0) \end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\bar{A} = \langle \Psi | \hat{A} | \Psi \rangle = \langle \Psi_0 | \hat{U}^*(t,t_0) \hat{A} \hat{U}(t,t_0) | \Psi_0 \rangle\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Heisenberg}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:heisenberg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\sphinxAtStartPar
for \(\hat{H}\) independent from time \(t\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dfrac{d}{dt} \bar{\mathbf{r}} & = \overline{\frac{i}{\hbar} \left[ \hat{H}, \hat{\mathbf{r}} \right]} \\
  \dfrac{d}{dt} \bar{\mathbf{p}} & = \overline{\frac{i}{\hbar} \left[ \hat{H}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} \right]} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Hamiltonian Mechanics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
From Lagrange equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = Q_q\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(q\) generalized coordinates, \(p:= \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}\) generalized momenta.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hamiltonian
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}H(p,q,t) = p \dot{q} - L(\dot{q}, q, t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Increment of the Hamiltonian
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}dH = \partial_p H dp + \partial_q H dq + \partial_t H dt \end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  dH & = \dot{q} dp + p d \dot{q} - \partial_{\dot{q}} L d \dot{q} - \partial_{q} L d q - \partial_t L d t = \\
     & = \dot{q} dp - \partial_{q} L d q - \partial_t L d t = \\
     & = \dot{q} dp - \left( \dot{p} + Q_q \right) d q - \partial_t L d t = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \frac{\partial H}{\partial p} = \dot{q} \\
  \frac{\partial H}{\partial q} = - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = - \dot{p} + Q_q \\
  \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} = - \frac{\partial L}{\partial t}
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Physical quantity \(f(p(t), q(t), t)\). Its time derivative reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\frac{d f}{dt}
  & = \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} \dot{p} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial q} \dot{q} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \\
  & = \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} \left[ - \frac{\partial H}{\partial q} + Q_q \right] + \frac{\partial f}{\partial q} \frac{\partial H}{\partial p} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \\
  & = \{ H, f \} + \partial_t f + Q_q \partial_p f
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(Q_q = 0\), the correspondence between quantum mechanics and classical mechanics
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{d f}{d t} = \{ H, f \} + \partial_t f \qquad \leftrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{d}{dt} \overline{\hat{f}} = \overline{\frac{i}{\hbar} [ \hat{H}, \hat{f} ]} + \overline{\frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial t}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\{ H, f \} \qquad \leftrightarrow \qquad \frac{i}{\hbar}[\hat{H}, \hat{f}]\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Attualization of 1925 papers}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:attualization-of-1925-papers}}


\sphinxAtStartPar
…to find the canonical commutation relation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} ] = i \hbar  \mathbb{I} \, \hat{\mathbf{1}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\left[ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} \right]
 & = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \hat{\mathbf{p}} - \hat{\mathbf{p}} \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \\
 & = \hat{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r} \hat{\mathbf{p}}
   - \hat{\mathbf{p}} \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r} \ \hat{\mathbf{r}} \ \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | d \mathbf{r}' = \\
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} - \hat{\mathbf{p}} \int_{\mathbf{r}} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \mathbf{r}' \underbrace{\langle \mathbf{r} |\mathbf{r}' \rangle}_{\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}')} \langle \mathbf{r}' | d \mathbf{r}' = \\
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} - \hat{\mathbf{p}} \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r} = \\
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} - \int_{\mathbf{r}'} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r} \ \hat{\mathbf{p}} \ \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \mathbf{r}' | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | d \mathbf{r}' = \\
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} | \, d \mathbf{r} + \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r} \int_{\mathbf{r}'} \mathbf{r}' | \mathbf{r}' \rangle \langle \mathbf{r}' | d \mathbf{r}' = \dots
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\left[ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} \right] | \Psi \rangle 
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} \mathbf{r} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) + \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \nabla \left( \mathbf{r} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \right) = \\
 & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle i \hbar \left[ \mathbf{r} \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) + \mathbb{I} \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) + \mathbf{r} \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{r},t) \right] = \\
 & = i \hbar \underbrace{\int_{\mathbf{r}} | \mathbf{r} \rangle \langle \mathbf{r} | d \mathbf{r}}_{\hat{\mathbf{1}}} \, | \Psi \rangle \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and since \(| \Psi \rangle\) is arbitrary
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{p}} \right] = i \hbar \mathbb{I} \hat{\mathbf{1}} \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \hat{r}_a, \hat{p}_b \right] = i \hbar \delta_{ab} \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Heisenberg Uncertainty relation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:heisenberg-uncertainty-relation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:quantum-mechanics-heisenber-uncertainty-relation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Uncertainty principle is a relation that holds for “wave descriptions” as it can be proved in the generic framework of \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/complex/fourier-transform.html}{Fourier transform}, see \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/complex/fourier-transform.html\#uncertainty-relation}{Fourier transform:Uncertainty relation}.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Heisenberg uncertainty relation is a relation between product of the variance of two physical quantities and their commutator,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{relation with measurement process and outcomes. Commutation as a measurement process: first measure \(B\) and then \(A\), or first measure \(A\) and then \(B\)}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_A \sigma_B \ge \frac{1}{2} \left|\overline{[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]}\right| \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof of Heisenberg uncertainty “principle”}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \sigma^2_A \sigma^2_B
 & = \langle \Psi | \left(\hat{A} - \bar{A} \right)^2 | \Psi \rangle\langle \Psi | \left(\hat{B} - \bar{B} \right)^2 | \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \langle (\hat{A} - \bar{A} ) \Psi |  (\hat{A} - \bar{A} ) \Psi \rangle \langle  (\hat{B} - \bar{B} ) \Psi |  (\hat{B} - \bar{B} ) \Psi \rangle = \\
 & = \| ( \hat{A} - \bar{A} ) \Psi \|^2 \| ( \hat{B} - \bar{B} ) \Psi \|^2 = \\
 & \ge \left| \langle ( \hat{A} - \bar{A} ) \Psi | ( \hat{B} - \bar{B} ) \Psi  \rangle \right|^2 = \\
 & = \left| \langle \Psi | (\hat{A} - \bar{A})(\hat{B} - \bar{B}) \Psi \rangle \right|^2 = \\
 & = \left| \langle \Psi | \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{A}\bar{B} - \bar{A}\hat{B} + \bar{A}\bar{B} | \Psi \rangle \right|^2 = \\
 & = \left| \langle \Psi | \hat{A}\hat{B} - \bar{A}\bar{B} | \Psi \rangle \right|^2 \ge && \text{(1)} \\
 & = \left| \frac{\langle \Psi | \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A} | \Psi \rangle}{2i} \right|^2 = \\
 & = \frac{ \left|\langle \Psi | [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] | \Psi \rangle \right|^2}{4} = \frac{1}{4} \left| \overline{[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]} \right|^2
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used Cauchy\sphinxhyphen{}Schwartz triangle inequality in (1),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}|z| \ge | \text{im}(z) | = \frac{z - z^*}{2 i} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}


\sphinxAtStartPar
Hesienberg uncertainty principles applied to position and momentum reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_{r_a} \sigma_{p_b} \ge \frac{1}{2} \left|\overline{[\hat{r}_a, \hat{p}_b]}\right| = \frac{\hbar}{2}  \delta_{ab} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Topics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics:topics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics:quantum-mechanics-history-topics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/topics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Atomic models.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1891, J.J.Thomson find electrons in cathodic rays. He found out that cathodic rays are made of negatively charged particles%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
While J.J.Thomson won the Nobel prize in Physics (1906) for having found the first sub\sphinxhyphen{}atomic particle, the electron, his son G.P.Thomson won the Noble prize (1937) for its discovery of the diffraction of electrons by crystals in 1927, thus showing wave behavior. Particle\sphinxhyphen{}wave duality never ends…
%
\end{footnote}, deflected by a transverse electromagnetic field. He:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
evaluated the ratio \(\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{el.charge}}\) of these particles. See \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-hs/ch/modern/experiments-matter.html\#scoperta-dell-elettrone-j-j-thomson}{Scoperta dell’elettrone \sphinxhyphen{} J.J.Thomson}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
proposed the pudding atomic model, with negatively charged particles in a positive cloud.

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1909, Rutherford scattering experiment and Rutherford atomic model: electrons around a compact nucleus

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1913, Bohr…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1916, Sommerfeld
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
relativistic model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
elliptial orbits

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
introduced another quantum number and degeneracy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
describe energy level split by magnetic field (Zeeman effect)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1925, Heisenberg and Schrodinger first theories about QM; Pauli solution of the \(\text{H}\) atom system

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectroscopy.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1707, Newton “Optics” described his experiments about diffraction of light with glass prisms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second half of the XIX century, experimental studies on the emission/absorption spectra in chemistry. Each element showed characteristics black lines in otherwise continuous absoprtion spectra (and corresponding bright lines in emission spectra, “hot spectra”)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Empirical laws for the refractive index followed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1836, Cauchy proposed a relation between the refractive index \(n\) of a material and the wave\sphinxhyphen{}length of the radiation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 = a + \frac{b}{\lambda^2} + \frac{c}{\lambda^4} + \dots \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with material\sphinxhyphen{}dependent parameters \(a\), \(b\), \(c\),…This model proposed \(n(\lambda)\) as a continuous function

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1870, Christiansen observed anomalous dispersion, with apparently discountinuous refractive index at wave lengths that are characteristics of the element under investigation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1872, Sellmeier proposed that anomalous dispersion should be described in the context of light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction, in terms of resonance modes of the matter and proposed his law for the refractive index
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 - 1 = \sum_{k} \frac{a_k \lambda_k^2}{\lambda^2 - \lambda^2_k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1875, Helmholtz modified Sellmeier formula, introducing a (wrong, this was not a dampening factor, as the one shown by Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model) dampening factor.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical-drude-lorentz}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model}}}}. Following the idea of Sellmeier, P.Drude (1900) and then H.Lorentz (1905) proposed a theoretical model for the refractive index of a medium, using a second\sphinxhyphen{}order damped oscillator, forced by the electric field of an incoming electromagnetic wave, and evaluated the transmitted wave as the sum of the incident wave and the one generated by the oscillating charges of the matter.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generalization of the Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model for systems with multiple modes became the general semi\sphinxhyphen{}empirical classical model for light dispersion
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n(\omega)-1 = \frac{q^2}{2 \varepsilon_0 m} \sum_k \frac{N_k}{\omega_k^2 - \omega^2 + i \gamma_k \omega_k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2(\omega) - 1 \simeq 2 \delta .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dispersion becomes quantum:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1905, Einstein explanation of photoelectric effect

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1906\sphinxhyphen{}1908, \sphinxstylestrong{Ladenburg} and Loria began experiments about spectral lines, anomalous dispersion, and the microstructure of the light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction. They found a way to measure the number density of the electrons responsible for spectral lines in absorption spectra in \(\text{H}\) atom (\(\text{H}_{\alpha}\) line only, while they had not enough accuracy for other weaker lines). Only few electrons resonate while the majority appear to be unaffected. They then focused on \(\text{Na}\) for better resolution. They came back to \(\text{H}\) few here laters (1911), to find \(\frac{N_{\text{H}_{\alpha}}}{N_{\text{H}}} \sim \frac{1}{50.000}\), \(\frac{N_{\text{H}_{\beta}}}{N_{\text{H}}} \sim \frac{1}{200.000}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1913, Bohr model (incompatible with classical mechanics, no \(e^-\) fast collapse on the nucleus, due to classical radiation):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
circular stable orbits with quantized angular momentum \(n h\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines are generated by quantum jumps, with \(\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
results compatible with the empirical Rydberg formula (1888)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ladenburg: how do both Bohr model and Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model work so well in atomic spectra?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1914, H.Kohn: experimental confirmed radiation emitted by incandescent bodies can be treated as thermal radiation. Ladenburg then used thermodynamics to explain thermal radiation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Still Ladenburg
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1914, procedure to compute the density of dispersion electrons

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1921, quantum counterpart of the classical dispersion, and link with Einstein coefficients (1916)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{physical atom is replaced by a representation of oscillators}: only frequencies and intensities of spectral lines can be observed. They abandoned the idea of building a “physical model of the atom” following the electron along an orbit, and built a model that’s just compatible with the phhysical quantities they can measure

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1924, \sphinxstylestrong{Kramers} (with theoretical derivation from Born, 1924, and Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rule for \sphinxstylestrong{polarization} with transition frequencies (both to higher and lower energy levels, modeling both emission and absorption)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kramers formula and the idea of virtual oscillators are used by Heisenberg in his formulation of matrix mechanics: this formula set the origin for the non\sphinxhyphen{}commutativity of physical quantities and, thus, Heisenberg uncertainty principle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tested by Ladenburg, 1928

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Radiation and Light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interaction.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1896, Wien’s law

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1900, Planck described the \sphinxstylestrong{continuous spectrum} of black\sphinxhyphen{}body radiation, introducing of \(h\), and the idea that light radiation with frequency \(\nu\) have discrete amount of energy, \(h \nu\). He first introduced \(h\) as a trick for matching experimental results of the spectrum \(\rho(\nu, T)\); a model of statistical mechanics of radiation with discrete levels of energy followed, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/statistical-mechanics/notes:statistical-mechanics-notes-distributions-be}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Black\sphinxhyphen{}body ratiation using Bose\sphinxhyphen{}Einstein statistics}}}}, even though that was the original way Planck first found a theoretical model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1905, Einstein explained the photolectric effects using Planck constant \(h\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1916, Einstein
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
derived Planck’s law from Bohr’s atomic model, using a (quantum) statistical approach to the interaction of atoms (and thier electrons) and electromagnetic radiation in a box. He postulated the existence of three processes, introducing proportionality \sphinxstylestrong{Einstein coefficients}, for transition probability (of a \(e^-\)) between states: \sphinxstyleemphasis{absorption} (rate: \(B_{kj} N_k \rho(\nu)\)) \sphinxstyleemphasis{spontaneous emission} (rate: \(-A_{jk} N_j\)), and \sphinxstylestrong{stimulated emission} (rate: \(- B_{jk} N_j \rho(\nu)\)). Stimulated emissions was found to be necessary in order for this model to be compatible with Planck’s law \(\rho \propto \frac{1}{e^{h\nu/k T}-1}\) for the system at thermal equilibrium (and not with Wien’s law \(\rho(\nu) \propto e^{-h \nu/ k T}\), the law one would get without stimulated emission)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Einstein couldn’t calculate his coefficients but he was positive that they could be computed once a theory about the atom had beenngwould be established

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
recognized that light quanta have momentum, \(p = \hbar k = h \frac{\nu}{c}\), then found by Compton (1923) in experiments about X\sphinxhyphen{}rays scattering

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in 1927, Dirac calculated Einstein coefficients (The Quantum Theory of Emission and Absorption of Radiation)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Origin of quantum mechanics.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix mechanics.} (Heisenberg, Born, Jordan), three papers in 1925

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ondulatory mechanics.} (Schrodinger)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1923, \sphinxhref{http://L.de}{L.de} Broglie: idea of guiding wave for matter particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1925, E.Schrodinger: wave equation. If matter behaves as a wave, a wave equation should be the governing equation of the system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1923\sphinxhyphen{}1927, C.Davisson and L.Germer found a diffraction pattern in an experiment about electron scattering

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equivalence.} (Dirac)

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Classical dispersion}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:classical-dispersion}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical}}

\subsubsection{Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:drude-lorentz-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/quantum-mechanics/history/light-dispersion:quantum-mechanics-history-dispersion-classical-drude-lorentz}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n(\omega)-1 = \frac{q^2 N}{2 \varepsilon_0 m} \frac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + i \gamVma \omega}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} The refractive index \(n\) is a complex number, with
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \text{re} \{ n \}(\omega) & = 1 + \Delta n_0 \omega^2_0 \frac{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega)^2 + \gamma^2 \omega^2} \\
  \text{im} \{ n \}(\omega) & = - \Delta n_0 \omega^2_0 \frac{\gamma \omega}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega)^2 + \gamma^2 \omega^2} \ \le 0 \ , \quad \forall \omega \ge 0 \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here the condition \(\omega \ge 0\) is required by the condition that the incoming wave travels from left to right.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, a travelling wave
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(x,t) = e^{i (\omega t - k x)} = e^{i \omega \left( t - \frac{x}{c} \right)} = e^{i \omega \left( t - n \frac{x}{c_0} \right)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
thus contains both a oscillating and a dampening contribution by \(n = \text{re}\{ n \} + i \, \text{im}\{ n \}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(x,t) = e^{\frac{\omega}{c_0} \text{im}\{ n(\omega) \} x} e^{i \omega \left( t - \text{re}\{ n(\omega) \} \frac{x}{c_0} \right)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the imaginary part of the refractive index is negative for all the positive frequencies, than the real exponential represents a damping term. The minimum value of \(\text{im}\{ n \}(\omega)\) for a slightly damped second\sphinxhyphen{}order oscillator occurs approximately at the natural frequency, \(\omega_{max damp} \simeq \omega_0\). This represents an \sphinxstylestrong{absorption of radiation} by the matter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} Drude\sphinxhyphen{}Lorentz model in the form \(n - 1 = \delta\) is compatible with empirical formulas in the form \(n^2 - 1 = \widetilde{\delta}\), as the correction is “small enough” for a linear approximation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n^2 = ( 1 + \delta )^2 \simeq 1 + 2 \delta \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Introduction to the QM of Solids}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:introduction-to-the-qm-of-solids}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm::doc}}

\subsection{Energy bands}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:energy-bands}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm-energy-bands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First, the energy level splitting is discussed. Then, two models (Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny, and nearly free electron models) are introduced to describe the concept of allowed and forbidden energy bands, starting from Schrodinger equation.


\subsubsection{Energy level splitting}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:energy-level-splitting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section deal with energy level splitting in a two\sphinxhyphen{}element system.
\subsubsection*{Non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting systems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(| L \rangle\), and \(| R \rangle\) two localized eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states of non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting identical subsystems, with the same energy \(E_0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{H}_0 | L \rangle & = E_0 | L \rangle  \\
  \hat{H}_0 | R \rangle & = E_0 | R \rangle  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As these states are localized in space, they’re (approximately?) orthogonal, \(\langle L | R \rangle = 0\).
\subsubsection*{Interacting subsystems \sphinxhyphen{} Perturbation potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the two systems are brought close together, they start interacting weakly, so that the Hamiltonian becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \hat{V} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The matrix elements of the Hamiltonian in the base \(\left\{ | L \rangle, | R \rangle \right\}\) (where are all the other eigen\sphinxhyphen{}functions? We’re not interested in them, right now, but only on the pair of eigenfunctions with the same energy when the syb\sphinxhyphen{}systems are not interacting) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \langle L | \hat{H} | L \rangle & =: E_0' \\
  \langle R | \hat{H} | R \rangle & =: E_0' \\
  \langle L | \hat{H} | R \rangle & = \langle R | \hat{H} | L \rangle^* =: -t \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Energy levels \sphinxhyphen{} Eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator }

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the new eigen\sphinxhyphen{}functions of the interacting system can be written as a linear combination of the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting functions, \(| \Psi_{1,2} \rangle= \ell_{1,2} | L \rangle + r_{1,2} | R \rangle\), the eigen\sphinxhyphen{}problem becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{H} | \Psi_{1,2} \rangle = E_{1,2} | \Psi_{1,2} \rangle \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Projecting onto \(\langle L |\), and \(\langle R |\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{cases}
     \ell E_0' - r t    = E \ell \\
   - \ell t    + r E_0' = E r    \\
\end{cases}
\quad \rightarrow \quad
\begin{cases}
     \ell (E_0'-E) - r t    = 0 \\
   - \ell t    + r (E_0'-E) = 0 \\
\end{cases}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This system has non trivial solutions, if the determinant of the linear system is zero,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \left| \begin{matrix} E_0' - E & -t \\ -t & E_0' - E \end{matrix}\right| = ( E_0' - E ) - t^2 \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy levels of the interacting states are slightly shifted w.r.t. the non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting level,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = E_0' \mp t \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{bonding state}, for \(E = E_0' - t\), \(\ell = -r\), and with normalization
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle_{-} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | L \rangle + | R \rangle \right) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{anti\sphinxhyphen{}bonding state}, for \(E = E_0' + t\), \(\ell = r\), and with normalization
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}| \Psi \rangle_{+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( | L \rangle - | R \rangle \right) \ \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny model}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:kronig-penny-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm-energy-bands-kronig-penny}}\subsubsection*{Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Kronig\sphinxhyphen{}Penny model is a 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional model with periodic square wave potential,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V(x) = \left\{\begin{aligned}
  V_0  \quad & , \quad x \in \text{regions II} = [ n a + (n-1) b, n ( a + b )]  \\
    0  \quad & , \quad x \in \text{regions I } = [ (n-1) (a+b), n a + (n-1) b] \\
\end{aligned}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{General expression of Bloch states}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/notes-solid-state:solid-state-crystals-bloch-thm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bloch’s theorem}}}}, the eigen\sphinxhyphen{}states of an electron (in position base) in a infinite periodic lattice can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(\mathbf{r}) = u(\mathbf{r}) e^{i \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(u(\mathbf{r}) = u \left(\mathbf{r} + \sum_j n_j \mathbf{a}_i \right)\) with the same periodicity as the lattice, \(n_j \in \mathbb{Z}\), or in 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Psi(x) = u(x) e^{i k x} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Eigenvalue problem for the Hamiltonian operator}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eigenvalue problem for the Hamiltonian operator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E \Psi = \hat{H}  \Psi = \left[ \frac{\hat{p}^2}{2m} + V(x) \right] \Psi \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\hat{p}\) the momentum operator, whose expression in position base is given by \eqref{equation:ch/quantum-mechanics/intro:eq:qm:momentum-operator}, and in 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems \(\hat{p} \Psi = - i \hbar \partial_x \Psi\). The operator acting twice gives \(\hat{p}^2 \Psi = - \hbar^2 \partial_{xx} \Psi\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing the expression of the eigenfunctions from Bloch’s theorem%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
The derivatives read \(\Psi' = \left( u' + i k u \right) e^{i k x}\), and \(\Psi'' = \left( u'' + 2 ik u' - k^2 u \right) e^{ikx}\).
%
\end{footnote}, it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E u(x) = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \left( u''(x) + 2 ik u'(x) - k^2 u(x)  \right) + V(x) u(x) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = u'' + 2 i k u'(x) - \left( k^2 - \frac{2m E}{\hbar^2} \right) u(x) && \text{regions I} \\
  0 & = u'' + 2 i k u'(x) - \left( k^2 - \frac{2m ( E - V_0 )}{\hbar^2} \right) u(x) && \text{regions II} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution of the ODEs.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Continuity of \(\Psi(x)\), and \(\partial_x \Psi(x)\).} for matching solutions.**

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Energy levels.}

\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:nearly-free-electron-model}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-solids-qm:semiconductors-solids-qm-energy-bands-nearly-free-electron}}

\subsection{Structure of a semi\sphinxhyphen{}semiconductor}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:structure-of-a-semi-semiconductor}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, \(N_A\), \(N_D\), \(N_A^-\), \(N_D^+\) only depends on the space coordinate, as a consequencen of doping. The concentration of free electrons and holes may be time dependent instead (…).


\subsubsection{Intrinsic semiconductor}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:intrinsic-semiconductor}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-intrinsic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Lattice of \(\text{Si}\) atoms. Some free electrons have left the valence bands of the atoms and entered the conduction band. For a new free electron, a new hole is left behind in the lattice. If the medium is \sphinxstylestrong{electrically neutral} the numbers of free electrons and holes are locally equal, and thus their concentrations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n_i(\mathbf{r}) = p_i(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Doped semiconductors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:doped-semiconductors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped}}

\paragraph{\protect\(p\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}type}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:p-type}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-p-type}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The semiconductor is doped with atoms of class \(\text{III}\), replacing some of the \(\text{Si}\) atoms in the lattice. These atoms introduce a hole in the lattice and are prone to collect \(e^-\) from neighboring \(\text{Si}\) atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization condition}}}}, all the doping atoms are ionized, and thus \(N_A^- = N_A\). In a \sphinxstylestrong{electrically netural} region with no donor atoms, the concentration of the holes is equal to the sum of the concentration of the ionized acceptor atoms and the free electrons,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = n + N_A^- \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In a standard \(p\)\sphinxhyphen{}type semiconductor, \(N_A >> n_i\), and thus \(p \sim N_A^-\).


\paragraph{\protect\(n\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}type}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:n-type}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-n-type}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The semiconductor is doped with atoms of class \(\text{V}\), replacing some of the \(\text{Si}\) atoms in the lattice. These atoms introduce a “extra” loosely bound electron in the lattice and are prone to release it in the conduction band of the semiconductor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization condition}}}}, all the doping atoms are ionized, and thus \(N_D^+ = N_D\). In a \sphinxstylestrong{electrically netural} region with no acceptor atoms, the concentration of the free electrons is equal to the sum of the concentration of the ionized donor atoms and holes,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}n = p + N_D^+ \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In a standard \(n\)\sphinxhyphen{}type semiconductor, \(N_D >> p_i\), and thus \(n \sim N_D^+\).


\paragraph{Full ionization}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:full-ionization}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo}


\subsection{Electric charge density}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:electric-charge-density}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-charge-density}}\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:eq:semi:charge-density}
\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{r},t) = -q n(\mathbf{r},t) + q p(\mathbf{r},t) + q N_D^+(\mathbf{r},t) - q N_A^-(\mathbf{r},t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(q\) the elementary charge, the charge of the electron (here the opposite to get a positive numerical value of \(q\) in Coulomb)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the mobile electrons

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the holes in the valence bands of the lattice

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N_D^+(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the positive donor ions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N_A^-(\mathbf{r},t)\) the number volume density of the negative acceptor ions

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, \(N_D^+(\mathbf{r})\), \(N_A^-(\mathbf{r})\), corresponding to the density of the donor and acceptor atoms in the lattice, that have fixed positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss the values of \(N_D^+\) and \(N_D\) in terms of energy levels at different temperatures.} Add this discussion to {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-equilibrium:semiconductors-equilibrium-structure-doped-full-ionization}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{full\sphinxhyphen{}ionization section}}}} or in another section and then point to it?

\subsection{Currents in semiconductors}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:currents-in-semiconductors}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-currents}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Two main processes:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{diffusion} due to non\sphinxhyphen{}uniform density

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{drift} due to an electric field \(\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r})\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The overall current has the contribution of the motion of both electrons (\(n\), for negative charges) and holes (\(p\), for positive “charges”),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r},t) = \mathbf{j}_n(\mathbf{r},t) + \mathbf{j}_p(\mathbf{r},t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and both these contributions have their diffusion and drift part,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_n & = \mathbf{j}_{n,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{n,drift} \\
  \mathbf{j}_p & = \mathbf{j}_{p,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{p,drift} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the contribution of the electrons, the diffusion current follows a Fick’s law for the number density \(n\) (multiplied by the constant charge \(-q\) of the elementary charge), while the drift coefficient is written as the product of the negative charge density and their drift velocity,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_n 
  & = \mathbf{j}_{n,diff} + \mathbf{j}_{n,drift} = \\
  & = - D_n (-q) \nabla n + \underbrace{(-q) n}_{\rho_n} \mathbf{v}_n = \\
  & = D_n q \nabla n + q \mu_n n \mathbf{e} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being the average drift velocity, \(\mathbf{v}_n = - \mu_n \mathbf{e}\), a function on the local electric field through the electron mobility \(\mu_n\). Here the minus sign follows the definition of the electron mobility with positive value, and from the opposite direction of the local electric field \(\mathbf{e}\) and the drift velocity of negative charges.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the contribution of the holes,
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{j}_p 
  & = - D_p q \nabla p + q \mu_p p \mathbf{e} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remark.} While charges in free\sphinxhyphen{}space have acceleration proportional to the electric field, in solids they have drift velocity proportional to the electric field, due to collisions with the lattice. This mechanism can be described in terms of conductivity \(\sigma\) (or its inverse, resistivity \(\rho_R\)) of the medium, similarly to Ohm’s law
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j} = \sigma \mathbf{e} \quad , \quad \mathbf{e} = \rho_R \mathbf{j} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the expression of the drift current, as the sum of the \(n\) and \(p\) contributions in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n} and \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p} respectively,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{j}_{drift} = q ( \mu_n n + \mu_p p ) \mathbf{e} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it immediatley follows the formula for the resistivity (and the conductivity)
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:resistivity}
\begin{split}\rho_R = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{1}{q (\mu_n n + \mu_p p)} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{See discussion about this relation in 5.1.4. Velocity Saturation}


\subsection{Einstein relation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:einstein-relation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-einstein-relation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:einstein-relation}
\begin{split}\frac{D_n}{\mu_n} = \frac{D_p}{\mu_p} = \frac{k T}{q} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Balance equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:balance-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:semiconductors-transport-phenomena-equations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The density of free electrons and holes are governed by the following PDEs
\begin{equation}\label{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:num-balance}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t n - \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathbf{j}_n}{q} \right) = ( G_n - R_n ) \\
  & \partial_t p + \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathbf{j}_p}{q} \right) = ( G_p - R_p ) \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the expression of current densities \(\mathbf{j}_n\), \(\mathbf{j}_p\) are given in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-n}, \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:charge-current-p} respectively, and the terms \(G_{n,p}\), \(R_{n,p}\) represent source and sink terms representing \sphinxstylestrong{generation} or \sphinxstylestrong{recombination} of free charges and holes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As for a new free electron there’s a new hole, then \(G_n = G_p\). As recombination occurs between the same number of free electrons and holes, \(R_n = R_g\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiplying the first and the second equation in \eqref{equation:ch/solid-state/semiconductors-transport-phenomena:eq:semi:num-balance} by \(-q\) and \(q\) respectively, the balance equation for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{free} charge density \(\rho_f = - q n + q p\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \rho_f + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope
